hero.title: PayPal buttons pattern
hero.description: PayPal offers two separate button products with similarly-shaped hosted-button IDs but mutually incompatible SDKs. A button created under one product renders nothing — or a misleading CORS error — under the other's component. Pick the mode below matching what PayPal's own dashboard gave the org.

donateButton.title: Donate Button (legacy)
donateButton.description: PayPal's original donate-sdk.js / PayPal.Donation.Button — only needs a hosted button ID and env, no client-id.

hostedButtons.title: Hosted Buttons
hostedButtons.description: PayPal's newer paypal.com/sdk/js?components=hosted-buttons / paypal.HostedButtons — needs both a client-id and a hosted button ID.

standard.title: Standard
items: Never assume which product an org's button ID belongs to from the ID's shape alone — check which embed snippet PayPal's dashboard actually gave them.
`donate-sdk.js` snippet (script src ends in `/donate/sdk/donate-sdk.js`) → PayPalDonateButton, see its dedicated page.
`paypal.com/sdk/js?...components=hosted-buttons` snippet → PayPalHostedButton, see its dedicated page.

A wrong/nonexistent hosted-button-id under the Hosted Buttons SDK surfaces as a CORS error (no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header on PayPal's backend response), not a clear "invalid ID" error — easy to misdiagnose as a domain-whitelist problem. Verify the ID with the exact literal snippet PayPal's dashboard provides before chasing CORS config.
Both components render non-breaking fallback messaging (a clearly labeled "not configured" box) when required props are missing, rather than a blank area.
